title: It wasn't the filter
spec: M08 · paste the failure, get the real cause
intro: One red test in TaskFlow, and every instinct says the priority filter is broken. It isn't. The bug is in the fixture that set the test up — and you find that by pasting evidence instead of guessing.

provenance.source: a narrated session against the shipped sample-project/taskflow; file paths, commands and the failure transcript are taken from the module, terminal output is reconstructed

foot: Run it for real: cd sample-project/taskflow && pytest tests/ -v

steps.title: Run the suite before you theorise
narrative: You are in sample-project/taskflow. Eight tests, seven green, one red. The red one is test_filter_by_priority_low: it asks GET /tasks/?priority=low for low-priority tasks and gets back three tasks of three different priorities.
Pipe the run to a file as well as the screen. You are about to paste this output verbatim, and retyping a traceback from memory is how you lose the one detail that solves it.
steps.youDo: cd sample-project/taskflow, then run the suite and tee the output to disk.

view.note: Seven tests pass. The one that fails is the only one that reads back what earlier tests wrote — remember that when you get to the diagnosis.

steps.title: Paste the evidence, not a paraphrase
narrative: Open the failure detail and look at what the assertion actually saw: three task dicts, ids 1, 2 and 3, priorities high, low and medium. The test created exactly one of them.

Now hand Gemini the raw output plus the two files it needs with @ references. @tests/conftest.py is the non-obvious one — most people attach only the failing test, which is precisely the file where the bug is not.
steps.youDo: Paste the failure into a gemini prompt and attach @tests/conftest.py alongside the failing test file.
steps.claudeSays: The @ references pull both files into the prompt as text. Gemini reads the fixture chain — client depends on db_session, auth_headers depends on client — before it looks at the endpoint.

gemini "This pytest output shows test_filter_by_priority_low failing:
FAILED tests/test_list_tasks.py::test_filter_by_priority_low
AssertionError: assert all(t['priority'] == 'low' for t in tasks)
tasks = [high task, low task, medium task — all three returned]
Look at @tests/conftest.py and @tests/test_list_tasks.py and diagnose
why the filter is returning all tasks instead of just low-priority ones."

steps.title: The diagnosis: the fixture, not the filter
narrative: Gemini's answer is the twist. routers/tasks.py is correct — query.filter(models.Task.priority == priority) does exactly what it says. The problem is that all three rows belong to the same testuser, in the same SQLite file, because nothing ever removed them.

Look at conftest.py: TEST_DATABASE_URL is a real file, test_taskflow.db, created once per session. The db_session fixture opens a session and closes it — close is not rollback. Every row an earlier test committed is still there when the next test runs.
That is why this failure is order-dependent. Run test_filter_by_priority_low on its own and it passes, which is the classic signature of a flaky test: green alone, red in the suite.
steps.claudeSays: Gemini returns the root cause and a drop-in replacement fixture: open a connection, begin a transaction, bind the session to that connection, and roll the transaction back in the finally block.

terminal.text:
Root cause: Test database isolation problem.

The conftest.py uses a single SQLite file (test_taskflow.db) and the
db_session fixture does NOT roll back between tests. Tasks created by
earlier tests (test_create_task, test_list_tasks_happy_path) persist
in the database when test_filter_by_priority_low runs.

When you call GET /tasks/?priority=low, the query correctly filters by
priority — but the "High task" and "Medium task" from previous tests
are still in the database under the same user (auth_headers creates
the same testuser every time).

Fix: wrap each test in a transaction and roll it back afterwards.

steps.title: Green — and it stays green in any order
narrative: Apply the fixture and re-run. Eight passed. Nothing in routers/tasks.py changed, because nothing in routers/tasks.py was wrong.

Toggle Before / After. The left panel is the database as test_filter_by_priority_low found it: two rows it never created. The right panel is the same moment after the rewrite — the transaction from every earlier test has been rolled back, so the only row present is the one this test wrote.

One honest caveat: rollback isolation fixes rows, not sequences. SQLite's AUTOINCREMENT counter and anything your app writes outside the session — a file, a cache, an env var — survive the rollback. If a test asserts id == 1, it will still surprise you.
steps.youDo: Apply the fixture, then run the suite twice: pytest tests/ -v and pytest tests/ -v -p no:randomly --lf
